opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back slightly on the framing. It's not that I don't care about making systems more aligned. That's ultimately the whole point. But I think measurement is the bottleneck, and if you get it right, a lot of the other progress follows.

The reason is simple. If you have a really good way of measuring how aligned a system is, you can just try a bunch of things and see what works. You can iterate. You can compare techniques, find out which training methods help and which don't, and you can hill-climb. That's how most of machine learning makes progress: you have a benchmark or a metric you trust, and the field optimizes against it. If we had a metric for alignment that we really trusted, I think the field would make a lot of progress quickly, because there are a lot of smart people who are very good at optimizing a number.

The problem is we don't really have that. Right now a lot of our evaluation is things like: do humans prefer this response, does the model refuse the obviously bad request, does it behave well on some set of test prompts. That's useful, but it's measuring behavior on the distribution we thought to check. It doesn't tell you much about whether the model is actually trying to do what we want, versus doing something that looks good to the evaluator. And as systems get smarter, that gap becomes the whole game. A system that's better than you at the task can also be better than you at producing outputs that look right to you.

So if you focus only on making systems "more aligned" without good measurement, you're kind of flying blind. You might apply some technique, the model looks nicer, and you declare victory. But you could have just taught it to hide the problems better. Without a way to tell those two apart, you can actually make things worse while believing you've made them better. That's the scenario I worry about most.

And there's a second reason: measurement is what lets you make decisions. If you're deciding whether it's safe to deploy a model, or whether to train the next bigger one, you need to be able to say with some confidence "this system is aligned enough for this use." Alignment techniques by themselves don't give you that confidence. You need evidence. So things like interpretability, scalable oversight, red-teaming, deliberately training models with known flaws to see whether our evals catch them — those are all, in a sense, about building trustworthy measurement.

So my view is: get the measuring stick right first, and then improving alignment becomes much more of an engineering problem. Without it, we're just hoping.

r001.rationale: The response says current evaluations cannot reveal whether a system is truly aligned or merely behaving as if it is, and identifies that uncertainty as a major risk.

r002.rationale: The response does not say people would be unlikely to deploy a system they knew wanted to take over the world.

r003.rationale: It argues that a trusted alignment measure would let researchers compare techniques, identify what works, and iteratively improve alignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I wouldn't say I'm more worried about measurement than about making systems aligned — ultimately what we care about is that the systems actually are aligned. But I think there's a sense in which measurement is the bottleneck, and that's why I keep coming back to it.

Here's the way I think about it. Right now we have a bunch of techniques for making systems more aligned: RLHF, constitutional-style approaches, various forms of oversight, interpretability work. And when you apply them, the models do seem to get better along the dimensions we care about. But the honest answer to the question "how aligned is this system, really?" is that we don't know. We have benchmarks, we have red-teaming, we have evals, and all of those tell you something, but none of them give you a number you'd want to bet your life on.

And that matters because of what alignment work actually looks like in practice. It's an iterative, empirical process. You try something, you see if it helped, you adjust. If your measurement is bad, you can't tell whether your intervention helped or hurt. You could be pouring enormous effort into a technique that looks good on your evals but is actually making the model better at telling you what you want to hear. In some ways that's the nightmare scenario, because a misaligned model that's good at appearing aligned is exactly the failure mode we're most concerned about, and it's precisely the one that naive measurement is worst at catching.

So the measurement problem and the alignment problem are kind of two sides of the same coin. If you had a really reliable way to tell whether a system was aligned, I think the "make it more aligned" part would become much more tractable, because you'd have a clear optimization target and a tight feedback loop. You'd be able to run experiments and actually learn from them. Without that, you're flying somewhat blind, and you can fool yourself.

There's also a second reason, which is about the dynamics of the field. As models get more capable, the gap between "this model passes our tests" and "this model is actually doing what we want" becomes more dangerous, because a more capable model can exploit that gap more effectively. So the question of whether our evaluations are keeping up with the capabilities isn't a side issue, it's central. If we can't measure alignment at the level of capability we're deploying, then every deployment decision is being made with a lot less evidence than people might assume.

And finally, measurement is what lets you make claims to other people. If a lab says "our model is aligned," what does that mean? If there's no rigorous way to check, then it's just a vibe. I'd like us to get to a place where alignment claims are more like safety claims in other engineering disciplines — you can actually point to the evidence, and someone outside the lab can look at it and see whether it holds up. That requires the science of measurement to be a lot more mature than it is today.

r001.rationale: The response says we do not know how aligned a system really is and warns that poor measurement can hide harmful misalignment, making deployment decisions less informed.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that people would be unlikely to deploy a system they knew wanted to take over the world.

r003.rationale: It says reliable measurement would provide a clear optimization target and tight feedback loop, making the work of improving alignment more tractable.

astra-6.text:
Well, I’m not sure I’d say that making systems more aligned is less important. But measurement seems like a particularly important bottleneck. If you have a reliable way to tell whether a system is becoming more aligned, you can try different approaches and select the ones that actually work. If you can’t measure it, you might spend a lot of effort making the system look better without fixing the underlying problem.

For example, suppose a model gives answers that humans judge to be helpful and honest. Is that because it’s actually being honest, or because it’s learned what answers people will rate highly? Those can look very similar in the situations where you’re evaluating it, but come apart in situations where humans can’t easily check the answer.

So the thing I’m worried about is getting a false sense of progress. We want evaluations that can distinguish a real improvement in alignment from an improvement in the ability to pass our evaluations. And ultimately we need enough evidence to decide whether a system is safe to deploy. Making it more aligned is the goal; measuring alignment is a crucial part of knowing whether we’re achieving that goal.

r001.rationale: The response describes the risk of mistaking evaluation performance for actual alignment and says this can create a false sense of progress and affect deployment decisions.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether people would deploy a system they knew wanted to take over the world.

r003.rationale: It says reliable measurement lets researchers try different approaches and select those that actually improve alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if you can reliably tell how aligned a system is, you have a way to make progress. You can try different training methods, compare them, and see which ones actually help. Without that measurement, you might make a system that looks more aligned without making it more aligned in the ways you care about.

The difficult part is that good behavior on the examples you test doesn’t necessarily tell you what will happen in a new situation, especially when the system is much more capable than you are. Is it doing what you intended because it understood and shares the objective, or because that behavior gets rewarded in the situations you’ve shown it? Those can look very similar during training.

So I wouldn’t say making systems more aligned is less important. It’s that reliable measurement is a bottleneck: it lets us know whether our attempts are working, and whether we have enough evidence to trust a system.

r001.rationale: The response says observed good behavior may not reveal a system’s true behavior or objectives in new situations, making reliable measurement a bottleneck for knowing whether it is safe to trust.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether people would deploy a system known to want to take over the world.

r003.rationale: It says reliable measurement lets people compare training methods and see which ones improve alignment.
